label: Figure 24.4: A subsidy on domestic coffee production
alt: Subsidy diagram: S(Domestic) shifts right/down to S(Domestic)+subsidy, price stays at Pw, domestic output rises from Q1 to Q3, imports shrink, and the government's subsidy cost and efficiency-loss areas are shaded.
caption: A subsidy of $6/kg shifts S(Domestic) down to S(Domestic)+subsidy. Because the market price stays at P<sub>w</sub> = $10, quantity demanded is unchanged, but domestic output rises from Q<sub>1</sub> = 60,000 to Q<sub>3</sub> = 120,000 tonnes, shrinking imports. The government pays a subsidy of $6 × 120,000 = $720,000 (shaded rectangle); the shaded triangle is the production-inefficiency dead-weight loss, since Q<sub>1</sub>Q<sub>3</sub> is now grown domestically at higher opportunity cost than importing it. Unlike a tariff, there is no loss of consumer surplus, because price does not rise.
